body: Pre-orders for some Apple Home Collection devices will open November 13
You can lock in orders for two LG cameras and a video doorbell.

On the same day that the Apple HomeView smart display and refreshed Apple TV 4K hit stores, pre-orders will open for some accessories in the Apple Home Collection. Apple confirmed to Engadget that you'll be able to pre-order the LG indoor camera, outdoor camera and video doorbell on November 13.

Those three devices, which Apple and LG collaborated on, will be the first Apple Home Collection accessories to ship. They're slated to arrive in December. Apple hasn't revealed exactly when other products in the lineup — including thermostats and door locks — will be available, but the company has said some will be available next month with the rest debuting in early 2027.

The indoor camera can capture 2.5K footage of what's going on in your home while you're away, giving you a way to keep an eye on your pets, for instance. It has low-light color night vision and infrared (IR) night vision support. The camera, which costs $200 and can detect people and pets, can tilt up when you're out and down when you're home — this can be managed automatically through the Home app or manually by pressing a button.

The outdoor camera can recognize faces, pets and deliveries. It too supports low-light color night vision, IR night vision and 2.5K video capture. The camera has IP65-rated protection from rain and dust and a two‑way talk function. As with the indoor camera, you'll get 10 days' worth of event video history via iCloud+. There's built-in storage too. The standard outdoor camera costs $300 and a version with a floodlight will run you $400.

As for the $250 video doorbell, that has a dual-camera design that can pick up (for instance) visitors and packages simultaneously — a 2.5K camera faces forward and a Full HD one points downward. You'll be able to view either feed separately in the Home app and chat to whoever's at your door using the two-way talk function. When someone rings the doorbell, HomeView and HomePod devices will sound a chime. You'll get notifications on other Apple devices too.

Again, there's low-light color night vision and IR night vision support, along with event video history in iCloud+ and built-in storage. The camera can detect people, pets, vehicles and packages and it has a dimmable spotlight.

Apple is making privacy a big selling point for these products, which offer end-to-end encryption (neither Apple nor LG will be able to access the data). Naturally, you can control them using your other Apple devices, such as your iPhone or HomeView, and view live video feeds.

articles.headline: If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do
keyFacts: ZDNET’s key takeaways - The November Windows update may fail to install on some PCs.
- People who installed the preview update seem to be affected.
- Microsoft is rolling out a fix to address the problem.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- The November Windows update may fail to install on some PCs.
- People who installed the preview update seem to be affected.
- Microsoft is rolling out a fix to address the problem.

Ah, Microsoft. Another Windows update, another glitch. This latest one affects some Windows 11 users who attempt to install this week’s November Patch Tuesday update, only for it to fail. But don’t worry, there’s already a fix in play.
On its support page to the November update designated KB5132061, Microsoft revealed and explained this latest problem.
More from ZDNET

Windows users who installed the November preview update released on October 28 may run into a glitch when trying to install the actual November update released on November 10. In this case, the installation may fail to complete. Your PC might repeatedly try to install the update or you may simply see an error code such as 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993.
I can confirm the problem. I installed the preview update on one of my Windows 11 virtual machines. Trying to then install the actual November update triggered the installation error.
If you’re in the same boat, what can you do to fix this dilemma? Just be patient.

Microsoft promises that all affected PCs should receive repairs within 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 1pm ET. For this, make sure your PC is connected to the internet and is set up to receive updates via Windows Update. Head to Settings and select Windows Update. You may already find the November update known as 2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974) available again. If so, select it to install it, and the process should work now.
Why would a problem like this occur?
Here’s how the update process works.
Microsoft typically releases each monthly Windows update in two phases.

First, there’s an optional preview update that kicks off around the end of the previous month. This one is considered a non-security update because it contains only feature changes. In this case, the preview update for November was released on October 28. Labeled KB5127936, this one unveiled the new customizable right-click menu, Cloud rebuild option, and other feature changes.
Second, there’s the actual mandatory Patch Tuesday update that contains both security patches and the non-security changes. Here, the November KB5132061 update was rolled out on November 10.

The preview updates are designed for IT administrators, software testers, and others who want an early look. That means they aren’t always fully baked and may contain a few bugs. But since they pop up in Windows Update, anyone can install them.
The actual Patch Tuesday updates are for all Windows users. In this case, there seemed to be an incompatibility or other conflict between the two updates that Microsoft then had to resolve.

articles.headline: Senator opens investigation into evidence RFK Jr ‘unlawfully lied’ to Congress
keyFacts: Democratic senators launched an investigation into evidence that HHS Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr lied to Congress about his Samoa trip.
Documented letters showed Kennedy's 2019 trip involved studying vaccines, contradicting his testimony that the visit was unrelated.
Children’s Health Defense has until 4 December to submit requested documents before lawmakers potentially issue subpoenas.
body: A top Democratic senator has launched an investigation into evidence that Robert F Kennedy Jr “unlawfully lied” in his 2025 confirmation hearings to become the US health secretary, citing a report by the Guardian.

Ron Wyden of Oregon, the incoming chair of the powerful Senate finance committee, is seeking extensive records from Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the non-profit anti-vaccine group Kennedy has used as a vehicle to fuel his political rise, including all documents related to a 2019 trip Kennedy took to Samoa.

“We are beginning an investigation into evidence that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy, Jr unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” Wyden said in a letter to the group that was sent on Wednesday and obtained by the Guardian. The letter was also signed by Angela Alsobrooks, a Democratic senator from Maryland.

In the letter, the two lawmakers cited reporting by the Guardian that indicated Kennedy lied about his reasons for going to Samoa in 2019, a trip that occurred just months before a measles outbreak killed 83 people in the Pacific island nation, mostly children under age five.

The trip, which Kennedy made as the chair and chief legal counsel of CHD, became one of the most criticized events in his career before he entered government. Critics, including Samoan officials, have said Kennedy’s presence emboldened anti-vaccine activists in Samoa, worsening a vaccination crisis. Kennedy has denied the allegations, saying he never gave any public statement about vaccines or discouraged Samoans from getting vaccinated.

“We are deeply concerned by the tactics Kennedy has used – both before and during his tenure as secretary – to stand in the way of children receiving life-saving vaccinations,” the two Democratic senators wrote. “In Samoa and in the United States, unvaccinated children have died tragic and preventable deaths during measles outbreaks. We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children. We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties.”
In two congressional confirmation hearings in January 2025, Kennedy told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation that his visit to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines”.

But letters obtained by the Guardian and the Associated Press through an open records lawsuit brought by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press contradicted that testimony. In one he wrote to the Samoan prime minister in January 2019 before the trip, Kennedy explicitly said he wanted to study the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the Pacific island nation. In it, he used the words “vaccine” or “vaccination” eight times.
The prime minister responded a month later, saying Samoa could benefit from CHD’s assessment of MMR vaccines and inviting him to come.
Children’s Health Defense did not respond to requests for comment, and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) did not immediately comment.

HHS previously said in response to the Guardian’s reporting on Kennedy’s Senate testimony that his visit to Samoa was “unrelated to vaccines. Any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory.” It has not provided a response to questions about why his testimony contradicted what he said in his letter to the Samoan prime minister.

By requesting documents from CHD, Wyden is aiming at the heart of Kennedy’s political machine. Since taking office, Kennedy has hired former CHD employees, including Lyn Redwood, a former CHD president who made early outreach on his behalf to Samoa. Redwood is now an employee at the HHS, reportedly working on vaccine safety. Kennedy’s closest adviser at HHS, Stefanie Spear, ran CHD’s newsletter before joining his 2024 presidential campaign.

With Kennedy now in government, CHD and its leaders often act as his most vociferous defenders, praising his work and explaining his decisions on their video podcasts, articles and on social media. Kennedy headlined CHD’s annual conference in September, where he made false and misleading claims about the safety of vaccines.

The Senate letter requested all documents related to any travel to Samoa by Kennedy or other employees or associates of CHD and any communications with Samoan government officials. It also asked for records related to Kennedy’s presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process.
In addition, the senators requested records related to Kennedy’s speech to CHD’s September convention and all communications between CHD and federal government officials since 20 January 2025.
CHD has a deadline of 4 December.

On the night of the election, after polls closed and it became clear Democrats would take a majority of seats in the Senate, Wyden made a social media post with a direct message about accountability. “Subpoenas,” he wrote, in the one-word post. Alsobrooks, a member of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, has repeatedly called on Kennedy to resign or be fired.

The letter does not go as far as the legal force of a subpoena. But it would be a good idea to treat such a letter seriously, said Tim Stretton, of the Project on Government Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog group in Washington.
“It’s not wise to ignore it,” Stretton said. “It’s really in their interest now to cooperate in a good faith effort.”
If they don’t, he said, the committee or chair could issue subpoenas to demand the information they are seeking.
Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence, though it is rarely prosecuted.

Wyden previously called for a criminal investigation of Kennedy’s testimony about his trip to Samoa. He said in August he would be pressing Republican colleagues to issue a criminal referral of Kennedy to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. He said then that “when Democrats retake the majority in the Senate, RFK will be at the top of the list of Trump officials the finance committee will hold accountable for endangering American families”.

Several other Democrats have called for Kennedy to resign or be impeached. Bernie Sanders, incoming chair of the Senate committee on health, education, labor and pensions, said he is open to impeachment. And the incoming senator Annie Andrews, a pediatrician from South Carolina, has been calling for Kennedy’s impeachment since her campaign.

Legal experts have said it is unlikely the justice department under Trump would prosecute, but said Kennedy’s statements could be used as grounds for hearings, for an impeachment inquiry or to create other obstacles for the Trump administration.

articles.headline: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
keyFacts: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance.
Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days.
Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times.
body: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.

These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.

Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

Google says the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.

The setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.

articles.headline: Jensen Huang To Step Down As Nvidia CEO Amid Affair Scandal
keyFacts: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down and exiting the board following reports of extramarital affairs.
The scandal involves a suspected Chinese spy, and Huang's departure plunges the $4 trillion chipmaker into uncertainty.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia looks for a permanent successor.
body: Nov 12 (Reuters) - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the AI industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chipmaker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said on Thursday. It named former Synopysys CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest shareholder with a stake of about 3.61%, will exit the board as well.
Nvidia shares fell more than 10% in premarket trading, and weighed on the broader market.
Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

Nvidia’s board met on Wednesday to consider his ouster, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Huang’s exit plunges the $4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia’s swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry’s biggest labs.
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.
Trump said on Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country” and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.
HUANG’S ROCK-STAR STATUS

For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips’ ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company.

That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies. Such is his pull that stocks moved at his mere mention of company names at events.

But scrutiny of his conduct has intensified in recent days after reports of his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed who U.S. authorities have concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The two, who have been photographed together in Taiwan, Singapore and California, are not related.

Washington has also investigated Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips, over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under U.S. export controls, according to media reports. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.
The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported to him.
(Reporting by Anhata Rooprai and Aditya Soni in Bengaluru;
Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila, Arun Koyyur and Saumyadeb Chakrabarty)

articles.headline: What the Democratic leadership fight is really about
keyFacts: Eleven House Democrats missed a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, causing the effort to fail and provoking leadership criticism.
Democratic lawmakers like Sen. Elissa Slotkin called for new party leadership beyond Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries following midterm victories.
Gabby Birenbaum said voters will watch closely to see if newly elected Texas Democrats deliver on promised improvements like lower costs.
body: Even in the event of a caucus led by Chuck Schumer, left, and Hakeem Jeffries, the pressure on congressional Democrats to meet the moment of voter anger won't disappear. | Win McNamee/Getty Images

Welcome to The Midterms, Actually, where every week I write about two things: one big idea or trend I see and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground. We’ll be taking a break for the rest of this year, but will be back to cover the key issues and people leading up to the 2028 election in the new year. Stay tuned!
One big idea

This Tuesday, just a week after voters delivered Democrats resounding midterm victories across the country behind a message of accountability and anti-corruption, Washington’s aversion to listening to voters reared its ugly head.

Eleven House Democrats missed a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, dooming the effort to fail and inflaming the calls for congressional Democrats to embrace new leaders , beyond Hakeem Jeffries in the House and Chuck Schumer in the Senate.

But the missed vote, which was condemned by progressives and moderates alike, also highlights a divide in the party beyond the traditional ideological camps. While “moderate” and “progressive” Democrats fight over which candidates performed better in last week’s midterms, and project those fights onto the congressional leadership debate, I’d say the bigger gap is between an anti-establishment electorate and a Washington blob stuck in the old ways of doing business.

Just think of what unified winning Democrats across the board on Election Day — candidates from James Talarico in Texas to Annie Andrews in South Carolina , from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Scott Colom, who leads a still-uncalled race in Mississippi — they didn’t just run against their Republican opponents, they ran against the status quo of both parties, and a political establishment that’s become too captured by outside interests and too self-satisfied with its approach to affect tangible change. The message wasn’t just that the economy is rigged against you, it was that the political system has also been rigged , captured by monied interests and a self-interested political class.

I’ve been a broken record on this point, but this is why I find it more helpful to see this election through the lens of top versus bottom, not right versus left. That is not just a framework that can help you see how Democrats succeeded electorally, but also explains how you get candidates like Colom in Mississippi or Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan now calling for a change in leadership.

Slotkin made the case for a bolder version of Democratic “moderates” on our podcast in October. “I don’t think the divide is moderate versus progressive, particularly in the era of Trump,” she told me. “I think it is fight versus flight.”

Then, at a press conference with Bernie Sanders on Tuesday, she called for a “ new generation of leadership .” She wants a leader who will govern for the whole caucus — blue, purple, and red states — and has asked for a full plan on the new majority’s priorities. Until then: “I’m a no until and unless I see that from anyone,” the Associated Press reported .

And here’s what said on this point back in March: “Leader Schumer, Leader Hakeem Jeffries, they’re both from the same borough,” Colom told Semafor , arguing the party needs leadership that understands rural America. Since the election, he has stayed noncommittal on Schumer , calling instead for more geographic diversity among party leaders, per the AP.

The charge for Democrats going forward wasn’t only about issues like anti-war, AI regulation, and lowering the cost of living, it was also to more robustly use the levers of power to frontally oppose this administration. One of Schumer’s biggest points of tension with Democrats was his refusal to shut down the government early in Trump’s term to challenge DOGE, and, later on, his failure to keep moderates united behind a shutdown that appeared to be putting real pressure on the administration to change its policies. That isn’t about right or left — that’s a call for more creativity on how politics are done.

I’m skeptical of the efforts to find a Jeffries or Schumer replacement in the short term. Washington works on access and relationships, first and foremost, and the uncomfortable reality is that, by the very nature of so many fresh faces, the anti-establishment wing of Democrats is at a deficit of options.

However, I’m fairly sure that even in the event of a Schumer- and Jeffries-led caucus, the pressure on congressional Democrats to meet the moment of voter anger won’t disappear. Because the Election Day win wasn’t just about the Democratic left, or its moderates, or arguments about electability — it was about change, and a voter-led outcry that is driven by backlash to this administration, but not solely defined by it.

It reminds me of what David Axelrod said on our show after the election . He reminded people that Democrats’ most successful electoral period — the Obama era — was built off an anti-establishment message, one that rejected the timidity, partisanship, and small-minded infighting between special interests that voters had come to loathe:

Barack Obama…was really fundamentally an anti-establishment candidacy. He was challenging the politics of both parties and the incumbent politics of Washington. … And I think that is the mood of the American people right now.
And here’s what he said about Jeffries/Schumer:

I’m not sure that they will take this advice, but I would be humble if I were them, because this victory was delivered by the American people. This victory wasn’t engineered in Washington. … They’re not sending people there to affirm status quo politics for Washington. They’re sending people there to change it.
Exactly.
What I’m hearing

Democrats won big around the country last week, but perhaps no state was more important — symbolically, politically, and substantively— than Texas. We asked the Texas Tribune’s Gabby Birenbaum to help walk us through just how an iconic red state swept Democrats into office up and down the ticket.

Texas has delivered Democratic wins for both Senate and governor. What are you hearing from people this morning, and was there a conversation or moment in your reporting that helped you understand how this happened?

I think there was very much an awareness that Talarico was in the driver’s seat for Senate, with cautious optimism from Democrats and concern from Republicans. But the idea of a statewide sweep was on the absolute far edge of people’s models, if on their radar at all. I think one of the biggest things I’ve been returning to today is what I heard from lifelong, more Bush/Cornyn-aligned Republicans on the trail this year. They couldn’t get there on Paxton. But more than that, a lot of them wanted to teach their party a lesson — that they should stop bullying them and then taking their votes for granted.
“People will be watching closely to see if their lives improve in the ways Democrats have promised.”

Talarico made his Christian faith central to his campaign, and there’s already talk of a resurgent religious left. How did that message land with the voters you spoke with? Did you see it reach people who wouldn’t ordinarily consider voting for a Democrat?

I think it worked in two ways. It gave a permission structure to nondenominational, more mainline Christians, especially soft Republicans and independents, to support him. And interestingly, Catholic Latino voters raised Talarico’s faith to me frequently. They said they appreciated that he was open about his faith.

Gina Hinojosa also defeated Greg Abbott. In your reporting, what connected these two victories? Were voters responding to the Democrats’ messages, turning against Republican leadership, or some combination—and which issues kept coming up?

I think asking for a fourth term is always difficult — especially so when people are frustrated about the economy. At the statewide level, one Republican described it to me as there being a Republican liability for every voter. Suburban moms were mad about Texas’s embrace of school vouchers. Seniors, veterans, and young people were mad about the THC ban. Rural voters were angry about data centers and the costs they felt in their communities of growth. And I think Hinojosa gave a lot of independents and soft Rs permission to vote for her by focusing on a populist, economic vision, jettisoning anything that could fall under culture wars.

The headline this morning is that Texas “turned blue.” From what you’re seeing locally, what does that description capture, and what does it miss? What are voters expecting these wins to change in their lives?

It undeniably did turn blue — it wasn’t one just one race, it was uniform. But I think what’s worth noting is that there are scores of Republicans and independents who decided, for the first time, to give Democrats a chance at the statewide level, for governor, or attorney general or even agriculture commissioner. People will be watching closely to see if their lives improve in the ways Democrats have promised — lower costs, better schools, rooting out corruption.
